problem: Session 83 established the CIA Triad as the language for what security protects. AAA — Authentication, Authorization, Accounting — is the operational framework that actually implements confidentiality and integrity in day-to-day system access. It answers three separate questions that get conflated constantly in casual conversation:
who are you, what are you allowed to do, and what did you actually do.

At FundedNext, this distinction matters concretely. An agent logging into the CEx Apps Script application proves who they are (authentication) via their Google account. Whether they can view KYC search results versus also edit refund records is a separate question (authorization) — and today, that boundary is largely implicit, resting on whoever was given edit access to the underlying Google Sheets rather than a deliberate, reviewed policy. And if a dispute arises over who changed a refund amount, the ability to answer it depends entirely on whether an accounting trail exists at all — which, as Session 82 highlighted, it currently does not in any durable form. The business problem AAA solves is making all three of these deliberate and separately verifiable, instead of one blurred assumption.

Cost of not doing it: conflating authentication with authorization leads to overprivileged accounts (anyone who can log in can do anything); missing accounting means disputes and incidents can never be conclusively resolved; and without all three working together, neither confidentiality nor integrity from the CIA Triad can actually be enforced or verified.
concept: AAA is a three-part framework used to control and record access to systems and resources. It originated in network access control (dial-up and RADIUS systems) but the same three-part logic now underlies essentially every access control model in enterprise IT, from AD to cloud IAM to the login screen of a web application.

Authentication: verifying that someone (or something) is who they claim to be. This is the 'prove it' step, and it can rely on something you know (password), something you have (a hardware token, a phone for MFA), something you are (biometrics), or increasingly a combination of these — tying directly into Session 65's MFA session still ahead in Layer 4's tail end and revisited here from a security-first angle.

Authorization: determining what an already-authenticated identity is permitted to do. Authorization always happens after authentication and is fundamentally a separate decision — proving you are Alice does not by itself say what Alice is allowed to access. This is enforced through mechanisms like ACLs, role-based access control (RBAC), and Group Policy (Session 60), and is the direct implementation layer for the Least Privilege principle coming in Session 85.

Accounting: recording what an authenticated, authorized identity actually did — which resources were accessed, what actions were taken, and when. This is effectively Session 82's centralized logging applied specifically to access and action events, and it's what makes authentication and authorization decisions auditable and disputes resolvable after the fact rather than only preventable in the moment.
A common shorthand: Authentication is a lock and key, Authorization is which rooms your key opens, and Accounting is the security camera footage of which rooms you actually walked into once inside.
deep: Authentication factors and protocols Authentication factors are categorized as knowledge (passwords, PINs), possession (hardware tokens, authenticator apps, smart cards), and inherence (fingerprints, facial recognition). True multi-factor authentication requires factors from at least two different categories — two passwords is not MFA, even though it's technically 'two things you know.' Underlying protocols that carry authentication include Kerberos (Session 54) and NTLM (Session 55) in Windows environments, and OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect in modern web and cloud contexts, where OAuth handles delegated authorization and OpenID Connect layers authentication on top of it.

Authorization models Discretionary Access Control (DAC) lets the resource owner decide who gets access — the model behind most Google Sheet sharing settings, including the CEx application's underlying sheets today. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) assigns permissions to roles rather than individuals, and users inherit permissions by being assigned a role — far more scalable and auditable than DAC as an organization grows, since you review roles instead of hundreds of individual grants. Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) goes further, making authorization decisions dynamically based on attributes of the user, resource, and context (e.g., 'only from a company network, only during business hours, only if department = CEx'). Mandatory Access Control (MAC) is the strictest model, where a central authority — not the resource owner — sets access rules that cannot be overridden, common in government/military contexts.

Accounting and audit trails Accounting protocols like RADIUS accounting and TACACS+ were originally built to log network access sessions (start time, duration, bytes transferred) for billing and audit purposes. In modern enterprise IT, the same concept shows up as audit logs (Session 82) capturing authentication events (login success/failure), authorization events (access granted/denied), and action events (what was read, created, modified, or deleted) — ideally all tagged with a consistent identity and timestamp so a single user's full session can be reconstructed.

AAA servers and centralization In larger networks, AAA is centralized through a dedicated server — RADIUS or TACACS+ — so that switches, VPN concentrators, and wireless access points all defer authentication, authorization, and accounting decisions to one system rather than maintaining separate local user databases. This mirrors the centralization argument made for logging in Session 82: scattered, per-device AAA decisions are much harder to audit or update consistently than one authoritative source.
workflow: A typical AAA transaction, regardless of the specific protocol, follows the same sequence:
Identity claim — the user or device presents credentials (username/password, certificate, token).
Authentication — the AAA system verifies the claim against a trusted identity store (e.g., Active Directory, an identity provider).
Session establishment — on success, a session or token is issued representing the now-verified identity.
Authorization check — for each subsequent action or resource request, the system checks whether this identity's assigned role/permissions allow it.
Access granted or denied — the requested action proceeds or is blocked, and either outcome is itself accounting-worthy information.
Accounting/logging — the authentication attempt, the authorization decision, and the resulting action are all recorded with identity, timestamp, and outcome.

Periodic review — access logs and role assignments are reviewed on a schedule to catch privilege creep (accounts accumulating more access over time than they currently need) and to revoke access no longer required.

The step most commonly skipped in informal environments — again including the CEx application as it exists today — is the last two: accounting is largely absent, and periodic review of who has edit access to which sheet does not currently happen on any defined schedule.
enterprise: AAA sits as the direct operational layer beneath the CIA Triad's confidentiality and integrity properties, and it spans policy, and audit discipline around that same machinery.

Organizationally, identity and access management (IAM) teams typically own the authentication and authorization infrastructure itself, security or compliance teams own the accounting/audit requirements and periodic access reviews, and individual resource or system owners (like a CEx team lead, in this context) are responsible for deciding who should be authorized for what within their own domain — a three-way split that mirrors AAA's own three-way structure.

At FundedNext: authentication for the CEx application is effectively handled by Google Workspace login (SSO, tying back to Session 64), authorization is handled informally through Google Sheet sharing permissions rather than a defined role model, and accounting is essentially absent — making this session's concepts a direct diagnostic checklist for where the application's access control currently stands relative to a mature AAA implementation.
dependencies: AAA depends heavily on infrastructure already covered across Layers 3 and 4:
Networking (Layer 3) — authentication traffic (Kerberos tickets, RADIUS packets) must traverse the network reliably and securely.
Directory Services, Active Directory, LDAP, Kerberos (Sessions 51–54) — the identity stores and protocols that authentication ultimately checks against.
Group Policy (Session 60) — a primary real-world mechanism for enforcing authorization decisions at scale in Windows environments.

Session 82 (Logging) — accounting is, in practice, logging applied specifically to authentication and authorization events; without a centralized logging pipeline, accounting has nowhere durable to live.
NTP (Session 69) — accounting records are only useful if their timestamps are trustworthy and consistent across systems.
dependents: AAA is a direct prerequisite for most of the rest of Layer 6:
Least Privilege (Session 85) — is fundamentally a policy about how authorization should be scoped; it cannot be implemented without a working authorization mechanism already in place.
Defense in Depth (Session 86) — treats AAA as one of several layered controls, assuming it already functions correctly on its own.
SIEM (Session 92) — authentication and authorization events (especially failures and anomalies) are among the most important log sources a SIEM correlates against.
Incident Response and Forensics (Sessions 100–101) — accounting records are frequently the first evidence reviewed to determine which identity did what during an incident.
Identity Governance (Session 66, Layer 4) — is essentially the ongoing-review discipline applied to authorization decisions made under this framework.
security: Authentication attacks: credential stuffing (reusing breached passwords), phishing (tricking a user into handing over credentials directly), and brute-force attacks all target the authentication step specifically; MFA (Session 65) is the single most effective mitigation against all three, since it requires an attacker to compromise more than one factor.

Authorization failures: the far more common real-world failure mode is not a broken lock but a lock that opens too many doors — overprivileged accounts, stale access nobody revoked after a role change, or a DAC model (like unmanaged Google Sheet sharing) where access sprawls informally over time with no central review. This is frequently a bigger practical risk than authentication weaknesses, because it doesn't require an attacker at all — it's simply unmanaged scope.

Accounting tampering: if accounting logs can be altered or deleted by the same accounts they're meant to hold accountable, accounting provides no real security value; this is the same tamper-evidence concern raised for logs generally in Session 82, applied specifically here to access records.

Separation of duties: a security best practice closely related to AAA is ensuring no single identity has both the authorization to perform a sensitive action and the sole ability to approve or review it — for example, the person who can edit refund amounts ideally should not be the only person who can review the accounting log of refund edits.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely AAA Failure First Check User can log in but can't perform an expected action Authorization gap — role/permission not granted despite valid authentication Check the specific permission or sharing setting for that resource, separate from login status User can't log in at all despite correct credentials Authentication failure — account lockout, expired credential, or identity provider issue Check account status and identity provider/SSO logs for the specific failure reason Dispute over who made a change, with no way to confirm Accounting gap — no audit trail exists for the action Confirm whether logging/accounting was enabled for that resource at all before the incident A former team member still has access weeks after leaving Authorization not revoked — stale access from missing periodic review Audit current access list against current team roster Login succeeds but authorization seems inconsistent across sessions Cached or stale authorization token not reflecting a recent role change Check token/session expiry and whether authorization is re- evaluated per request or only at login The recurring pattern worth internalizing: authentication problems are usually loud and immediate (can't log in at all), while authorization and accounting problems are usually quiet and only surface later, often during a dispute or audit — which is exactly why they're the two most commonly neglected in informal systems.
example: Consider a retail company where a former employee's VPN account was never deauthorized after their departure.

Authentication still worked (the credential was technically still valid), and it took a routine quarterly access review — not a real-time alert — to notice the account was still authorized for internal systems weeks later. No breach necessarily occurred, but the exposure window existed entirely because authorization revocation and accounting review were treated as optional cleanup rather than a required, scheduled AAA discipline.

The FundedNext parallel: if an agent transfers teams or leaves FundedNext, their access to the CEx application's underlying Google Sheets is only as good as whoever remembers to update sharing settings — there is currently no scheduled review step confirming that authorization matches the current team roster, and no accounting trail that would reveal if stale access were ever actually used. Applying the retail example's lesson directly, a simple recurring reminder to audit sheet access against the current CEx roster would close a real, currently-open gap.
cloud: Cloud IAM systems (AWS IAM, Google Cloud IAM, Azure AD/Entra ID) are AAA made explicit and code- defined: authentication is handled by the identity provider, authorization is expressed as policies (often JSON documents) attached to roles rather than individuals, and accounting is provided natively through services like AWS CloudTrail or Google Cloud Audit Logs, which record every API call with the calling identity, timestamp, and outcome by default.

A defining cloud-era shift is that authorization increasingly moves toward policy-as-code — permissions defined in version-controlled files, reviewed via pull request like application code — rather than being changed ad hoc through a console, directly addressing the stale-access problem from the Real Enterprise Example by making every authorization change visible and reviewable before it takes effect. Google Workspace, which underlies the CEx application's own authentication today, has its own admin-level audit log equivalent (Google Workspace Admin Audit Log) that could, with proper configuration, provide a real accounting layer without building anything custom.
automation: AAA maps directly onto concrete, buildable improvements for the CEx application, extending the logging foundation from Session 82:
Authentication — no action needed beyond what Google Workspace SSO already provides, but confirming MFA is enforced organization-wide (Session 65) is a cheap, high-value check.

Authorization — a scheduled script that periodically reads current sharing permissions on the KYC, refund, and ethics-email sheets and compares them against a maintained list of who should have access, flagging discrepancies automatically instead of relying on someone remembering to check.

Accounting — directly extending Session 82's logging wrapper, every Code.gs function that performs a sensitive action (viewing KYC results, editing a refund record) should log the acting user's identity (available via Session.getActiveUser() in Apps Script) alongside the action and outcome, finally giving the application a real accounting trail.

Together, these three automations would take the CEx application from today's implicit, unaudited access model to a lightweight but genuine AAA implementation, without requiring any new platform beyond what's already in use.
career: AAA is one of the most consistently tested frameworks in security and networking certifications and interviews, precisely because it's the operational backbone beneath almost every access control conversation — RBAC, least privilege, audit compliance, and IAM design all assume fluency with AAA's three-part structure.

For someone with a CEx support background, being able to describe not just that the application 'has access control' but specifically how authentication, authorization, and accounting are each handled (or currently aren't) is a much stronger, more credible signal in an interview than a vague description — it shows the ability to decompose a real system using an industry-standard framework rather than describing it only in its own informal terms.
Certification relevance: AAA is explicitly named and tested in Security+, Network+, and CISSP;
RBAC/ABAC/DAC/MAC distinctions specifically are a near-guaranteed exam and interview topic across all major security certifications.
interview: What are the three components of AAA, and how does each map to a different security question?
Why is authorization a separate decision from authentication, even though they often happen back-to-back?
Compare RBAC, ABAC, DAC, and MAC — when would you choose each?
Why is accounting often the most neglected of the three components in real systems?
What is separation of duties, and how does it relate to AAA?
Describe how RADIUS or TACACS+ centralizes AAA decisions across many network devices.
Why is MFA specifically an authentication-layer control, not an authorization-layer one?
How would you detect and remediate privilege creep in an organization with hundreds of employees?
What's the security risk of authorization changes being made outside of a reviewable, logged process?
Walk through what accounting data you'd want in order to investigate a disputed data change.
misconceptions: "If you can log in, you should be able to do most things": this collapses authorization into authentication; being verified as yourself says nothing about what you should be permitted to do, and conflating the two is exactly how overprivileged access accumulates.

"MFA solves authorization and accounting too": MFA is purely an authentication-strengthening control; a compromised but properly-MFA'd account can still cause damage if authorization is too broad or accounting doesn't exist to catch it.

"Accounting is only useful after something goes wrong": regular review of accounting/audit data (not just incident-triggered review) is what catches privilege creep and stale access before they become an incident in the first place.

"DAC (owner-controlled sharing) doesn't scale badly for small teams": even small teams accumulate sharing drift faster than expected once multiple people have edit rights to grant further access — the CEx application's current sheet-sharing model is a live example of this.

"Authorization, once granted, stays correct until someone complains": authorization correctness decays over time as people change roles or leave; without scheduled review, 'correct at the time it was granted' silently becomes 'wrong and unnoticed.'
anchors: Authentication = who are you (the lock and key). Authorization = what can you do (which rooms the key opens). Accounting = what did you actually do (the camera footage).
Two passwords is not MFA — true multi-factor requires two different categories: know, have, are.

Authentication failures are loud (can't log in); authorization and accounting failures are quiet (too much access, or no record) — the quiet ones are the ones that need scheduled review, not just alerts.
RBAC scales because you review roles, not hundreds of individual grants — DAC (owner-controlled sharing) scales badly precisely because it skips that abstraction.
If the same account can both perform a sensitive action and erase the record of it, accounting isn't providing real security value — separation of duties is what fixes this.
connections: AAA operationalizes the CIA Triad from Session 83 and draws together nearly all of Layer 4's identity concepts under a security-first framing.
Session 83 (CIA Triad) — authentication and authorization primarily implement confidentiality and integrity; accounting primarily implements integrity by making unauthorized changes detectable.
Sessions 51–55 (Directory Services, Active Directory, LDAP, Kerberos, NTLM) — the concrete authentication protocols and identity stores that AAA's authentication step relies on.
Session 60 (Group Policy) — a primary real-world authorization enforcement mechanism in Windows environments.

Session 64 (SSO) and Session 65 (MFA) — both are authentication-layer enhancements to the AAA model, already scheduled later in Layer 4 and directly relevant to how CEx agents log into the Apps Script application today.
Session 82 (Logging) — accounting is logging applied specifically to access and action events; the two sessions describe the same underlying mechanism from different angles.
Looking ahead to Session 85 (Least Privilege) — a direct policy layer on top of the authorization mechanism introduced here.
Looking ahead to Session 66 (Identity Governance, Layer 4) — the ongoing-review discipline that keeps authorization decisions accurate over time.

The FundedNext CEx application — authentication via Google SSO, informal DAC-style authorization via sheet sharing, and largely absent accounting together form a real, personally relevant case study for every concept in this session.

[ User presents credentials ] --> [ Authentication: identity verified? ] --(yes)--> [ Session/token issued ] -->
[ Authorization: is this action allowed for this identity? ] --(yes)--> [ Action performed ] --> [ Accounting: identity +

DAC: resource owner decides access (flexible, hard to audit at scale) | RBAC: permissions attached to roles, users

lab: This lab applies AAA directly to the FundedNext CEx application, producing real security artifacts rather than a purely theoretical exercise, and can be done alongside the ongoing home-lab VM from prior sessions for the protocol-level portion.

Step 1 — On the home lab VM, install and configure FreeRADIUS (a free, open-source RADIUS server) and configure it with two test users with different authorization attributes, to see authentication and authorization handled as genuinely separate steps in a real protocol.

Step 2 — Use a RADIUS test client (e.g., `radtest`) to authenticate as each user and observe the Access- Accept/Access-Reject responses and any returned authorization attributes, confirming the sequence from Diagram 1 end-to-end.
Step 3 — Enable RADIUS accounting in the same FreeRADIUS setup and confirm accounting packets are logged, giving a concrete look at what a real accounting record contains.

Step 4 — Back in the actual CEx Apps Script project, list every current editor/viewer on the KYC, refund, and ethics-email sheets, and compare that list against who currently needs that access — document any discrepancy found, however small.

Step 5 — Add a minimal accounting wrapper to one sensitive Code.gs function (e.g., refund lookup) that logs `Session.getActiveUser().getEmail()`, the action, and a timestamp to a dedicated Access Log sheet, giving that one function a real, working accounting trail for the first time.
Step 4 in particular often surfaces at least one real, previously invisible authorization gap — this lab tends to produce an immediate, concrete finding rather than only a training exercise.
